p.src: Now, when Grand Marshal Gao caught sight of the troops on the waterways, he knew the battle was lost. Just as he was about to withdraw, cannon fire sounded on every side. He hastily rallied his commanders and fled by whatever road he could find. In truth, the men of Liangshan Marsh had merely fired signal cannon all around and had laid no ambush at all. Yet Grand Marshal Gao was so terrified that he scurried away like a rat and bolted like a wolf, withdrawing his army through the night to Jizhou. When the infantry were counted, their losses proved slight; but more than half the naval force had been lost, and not a single warship returned. Liu Menglong barely escaped with his life and made it back. The soldiers who could swim escaped alive, while those who could not were all drowned. Grand Marshal Gao's military prestige had suffered a severe blow and his fighting spirit was crushed. For the time being, he quartered his forces inside the city and waited for Niu Bangxi to arrive with the requisitioned vessels. He sent another messenger with official orders to press the matter: regardless of kind, every serviceable vessel was to be seized and conveyed to Jizhou, where the force would regroup for a renewed advance.

p.src: Now Grand Marshal Gao assembled his commanders inside Jizhou and discussed how Liangshan might be suppressed. Among them, Xu Jing, Military Governor of Shangdang, reported: “When I was young, I wandered the rivers and lakes, demonstrating my spearcraft and selling medicines, and during that time I became acquainted with a certain man. He is deeply versed in strategy and thoroughly understands the art of war. He possesses the talents of Sun and Wu and the wisdom and cunning of Zhuge. His surname is Wen and his given name Huanzhang; he now teaches at a village school in Anren, outside the Eastern Capital. If we could bring this man here as an adviser, he could counter Wu Yong's cunning schemes.” On hearing this, Grand Marshal Gao dispatched a senior officer with bolts of silk and a saddled horse. The man hastened by night to the Eastern Capital and courteously invited Wen Huanzhang, the village schoolmaster and scholar, to serve as military adviser at the front. He was to proceed to Jizhou without delay and assist in directing military affairs. The senior officer departed for the capital, but before even three or five days had passed, a report came from outside the city that Song Jiang's army had advanced to the walls and was challenging them to battle. Grand Marshal Gao flew into a rage at the news. He immediately mustered the troops under his direct command and marched out of the city to meet the enemy, ordering the military governors of every camp to join him in battle.

p.src: When Song Jiang's forces saw Grand Marshal Gao approaching at the head of his army, they hurriedly withdrew fifteen li to a broad, open plain. Grand Marshal Gao led his army in pursuit, but Song Jiang's troops had already drawn up their battle formation beside a hillside. From the ranks beneath the red banners emerged a fierce commander. The standard bearing his title plainly identified him as Huyan Zhuo, the Double Clubs. Reining in his horse, he held his spear crosswise and took his place before the formation. At the sight of him, Grand Marshal Gao said, “That scoundrel is the man who rebelled against the court when he commanded the chain-armored cavalry.” He ordered Han Cunbao, Military Governor of Yunzhong, to ride out and engage him. Han Cunbao was highly skilled with a decorated halberd. The two met before the formations and exchanged not a single word: one thrust with his halberd, and the other met him with his spear. After they had fought more than fifty bouts, Huyan Zhuo feigned an opening, slipped away, spurred his horse, and fled down the hillside. Eager to win glory, Han Cunbao galloped hard in pursuit. The eight hooves flew like tumbling cups and scattered cymbals. After a chase of some five or seven li into a deserted place, Han Cunbao was nearly upon him. Huyan Zhuo then reined his horse around, shifted his spear aside, and came to meet him wielding his twin clubs. They fought another dozen or more bouts. Huyan Zhuo used his twin clubs to force the halberd aside, then wheeled his horse and fled once more. Han Cunbao thought, “The scoundrel's spear cannot get near me, and his clubs cannot best me. If I do not catch him here and take him alive, what better chance shall I ever have?” He charged after him, but upon rounding a spur of the hill he found two roads and had no idea where Huyan Zhuo had gone. Han Cunbao reined in his horse and climbed the slope to look around. There he saw Huyan Zhuo riding along a stream. Cunbao shouted, “You wretched brigand! Where do you think you are going? Dismount at once and surrender, and I shall spare your life!” Huyan Zhuo stopped and hurled abuse at Cunbao. Han Cunbao made a wide circuit to cut off Huyan Zhuo's retreat. The two came face-to-face beside the stream. A mountain rose on one side and the stream ran on the other, leaving only a single road between them, too narrow for the two horses to maneuver. Huyan Zhuo said, “If you do not surrender to me now, what are you waiting for?” Han Cunbao replied, “You are a defeated foe at my mercy, yet you ask me to surrender to you?” Huyan Zhuo said, “I lured you all the way here precisely so that I could take you alive. Your life will be over in a matter of moments!” Han Cunbao said, “It is I who have come to take you alive!” Their old fury flared anew. Han Cunbao leveled his long halberd and thrust at Huyan Zhuo's chest, ribs, and unarmored belly in a rain of blows. Huyan Zhuo knocked the weapon aside to left and right with his spear, then drove his own thrusts in like a tearing gale. They fought for another thirty bouts or so. As the fight reached its fiercest pitch, Han Cunbao thrust his halberd at Huyan Zhuo's unguarded ribs, while Huyan Zhuo drove his spear at Han Cunbao's chest. Each twisted his body aside, and both weapons shot beneath the other's arm. Huyan Zhuo pinned the shaft of Han Cunbao's halberd beneath his arm, while Han Cunbao seized the shaft of Huyan Zhuo's spear. Still mounted, each tugged and hauled at the other, gripping around the waist and hips and straining with all his might. The hind hooves of Han Cunbao's horse slipped down into the stream, dragging Huyan Zhuo, horse and all, into the water as well. The two men grappled together in the stream. The two horses sent water splashing everywhere, drenching both men from head to foot. Huyan Zhuo dropped his spear, clamped the shaft of the halberd under his arm, and hastily reached for his clubs. Han Cunbao likewise released Huyan Zhuo's spear shaft and seized both his arms. Tugging and grappling with each other, they both tumbled into the water. The two horses sprang up onto the bank like shooting sparks and galloped away toward the mountain. As the two men rolled about in the stream, they lost all their weapons and the helmets from their heads; their clothes and armor hung loose and bedraggled. With nothing but their bare fists, they fought on in the water, trading blow for blow, first in the depths and then dragging each other back into the shallows.

p.src: Just as the struggle remained deadlocked, a company of horsemen rushed up along the bank, led by Zhang Qing, the Featherless Arrow. They all joined in and captured Han Cunbao alive. Men were hurriedly sent to find the two warhorses that had run off. Hearing the neighing of horses and the shouts of men, however, the animals had themselves come running back in search of the troop and were thus recovered. They also retrieved the weapons from the stream and returned them to Huyan Zhuo. Still dripping wet, he mounted, while Han Cunbao was bound with his arms twisted behind him and laid across a horse; then they all made for the mouth of the ravine. Ahead they saw a company of soldiers coming in search of Han Cunbao, and the two forces met head-on. At their head were two military governors, Mei Zhan and Zhang Kai. Seeing Han Cunbao bound soaking wet upon a horse, Mei Zhan flew into a rage, brandished his three-pointed, double-edged blade, and charged straight at Zhang Qing. Before they had exchanged three bouts, Zhang Qing turned and fled. Mei Zhan pursued, whereupon Zhang Qing lightly stretched his gibbon arm, deftly twisted his wolfish waist, and sent a stone flying. It struck Mei Zhan squarely on the brow; blood spurted out, and he dropped his blade and covered his face with both hands. Zhang Qing wheeled his horse at once, but Zhang Kai had already nocked an arrow. He drew his bow to the full and loosed. Zhang Qing jerked up his mount's head, and the arrow struck it squarely in the eye, bringing the horse down. Zhang Qing leapt aside, gripped his spear, and came on to fight on foot. Zhang Qing's true skill lay only in felling officers with flying stones; with the spear he was rather slow. Zhang Kai first rescued Mei Zhan, then came back to fight Zhang Qing. Zhang Kai's spear, wielded from horseback, struck with uncanny and unpredictable skill. Zhang Qing could only parry; unable to hold him off, he trailed his spear and fled into the cavalry ranks for cover. Wherever Zhang Kai's horse and spear went, he slew fifty or sixty cavalrymen, scattering them in all directions, and recaptured Han Cunbao. Just as Zhang Kai was about to return, a tremendous roar arose. Two forces came from the ravine mouth: one led by Qin Ming, the Thunderbolt, and the other by Guan Sheng, the Great Blade. The two fierce generals charged in. Zhang Kai barely managed to escort Mei Zhan away. The two enemy forces charged in from either side and seized Han Cunbao once more. Zhang Qing seized another horse, while Huyan Zhuo, exhausting his remaining strength, could do no more than fight alongside the others. Together they drove the attack up to the government army's lines and, pressing their advantage, threw the troops into disorder and forced them back to Jizhou. The Liangshan forces did not pursue. That very night they merely escorted Han Cunbao up to the stronghold.

p.src: Song Jiang and the others were seated in the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness when Han Cunbao was brought in bound. Song Jiang ordered the soldiers away, personally untied him, invited him to sit in the hall, and treated him with every courtesy. Han Cunbao was overwhelmed with gratitude. Dang Shixiong was then invited out to meet him, and the two were entertained together. Song Jiang said, “Generals, harbor no suspicions. We have no rebellious intent; corrupt officials and venal clerks alone have driven us to this pass. If the court would pardon and enlist us, we would gladly exert ourselves in the service of the realm.” Han Cunbao said, “When Grand Commandant Chen previously brought an imperial edict of amnesty to the mountain, why did you not seize the opportunity to forsake evil and return to the right path?” Song Jiang replied, “The imperial edict itself was ambiguously worded, and village wine had been substituted for the imperial wine. For these reasons none of the brothers could accept it. Those two administrative officers surnamed Zhang and Commissioner Li abused their authority and humiliated our commanders. …” Han Cunbao said, “The whole affair failed only because there was no decent man between the two sides to manage it, and thus a great matter of state was ruined.” Song Jiang laid on a banquet for them. The next day, horses and saddles were prepared, and they were escorted out through the valley mouth. On the road, the two spoke at length of Song Jiang's virtues. By the time they reached the outskirts of Jizhou, it was already late. Early the next morning they entered the city, went before Grand Commandant Gao, and reported that Song Jiang had released the two commanders. Gao Qiu flew into a rage. “This is a rebel trick to undermine the spirit of my army. How dare you two show your faces before me! Guards, take them out and behead them, then report back to me!” Wang Huan and the other officers all knelt and pleaded, “This was no fault of these two men, but a scheme devised by Song Jiang and Wu Yong. If you execute them, the rebels will only laugh at us.” Beset by everyone's earnest pleas, Grand Commandant Gao spared their lives, stripped them of their offices, and sent them back to the Taiyi Temple in the Eastern Capital to await judgment. The two were escorted back to the capital.

p.src: We shall leave Wen Huanzhang departing the capital with the imperial envoy and speak instead of Grand Commandant Gao, who remained troubled in Jizhou. A gate attendant reported, “Niu Bangxi has arrived!” Grand Commandant Gao ordered him admitted at once and, when the formal greetings were over, asked, “What of the boats?” Bangxi reported, “Along the way I requisitioned more than fifteen hundred vessels, large and small. All have reached the sluice.” The Grand Commandant was delighted. After rewarding Niu Bangxi, he issued orders to release all the vessels into the broad harbor, fasten them together in rows of three, lay planks across their decks, and secure their sterns with iron rings. All the infantry were sent aboard; the remaining cavalry escorted the vessels along the water's edge. By the time the soldiers had been assigned to the boats and drilled to proficiency, half a month had passed, and everyone at Liangshan Marsh knew of it. Wu Yong summoned Liu Tang, gave him his instructions, and placed him in charge of winning merit on the waterways. The naval chiefs each prepared small boats whose bows were reinforced in rows with iron plates. The holds were loaded with reeds and dry firewood, into which sulfur, saltpeter, and other incendiary materials were packed; the vessels were then stationed in the narrow inlets. The artillerist Ling Zhen was ordered to fire cannon from the high hills commanding all four directions as the signal; among the tangled trees by the water they tied banners to the branches, set up gongs, drums, and cannon at every point, and made a show of stationed troops and fortified camps; Gongsun Sheng was asked to perform rites to summon the wind; and three bodies of troops were deployed on dry land to provide support. Thus Wu Yong completed all his dispositions.

p.src: Now Grand Marshal Gao mustered the troops at Jizhou. Command of the naval forces was entrusted to Niu Bangxi, together with Liu Menglong and Dang Shiying. Grand Marshal Gao donned his armor and ordered three rolls of the drums. The ships set out from the harbor and the cavalry advanced overland; the vessels sped like arrows and the horses flew like the wind as they charged toward Liangshan Marsh. First, as for the vessels on the water: their punting poles followed one another without a break, while gongs and drums sounded together. They pressed steadily into the depths of Liangshan Marsh, yet saw not a single boat. As they drew near Golden Sands Beach, they saw two fishing boats among the lotus beds. Each held only two men, who clapped their hands and laughed aloud. From the leading ship, Liu Menglong ordered his men to loose a volley of arrows. The fishermen all leapt into the water and disappeared beneath the surface. Liu Menglong urgently drove the warships onward. As they neared Golden Sands Beach, a dark line of slender willows stretched along the shore. Two yellow oxen were tethered to the trees, and three or four cowherd boys slept on the green turf. Farther off, another boy approached riding backward on a yellow ox, plaintively playing a flute. Liu Menglong ordered the bravest men in the vanguard to be the first ashore. The cowherd boys sprang up, laughing heartily, and vanished deep into the shade of the willows. Five or seven hundred men of the vanguard rushed ashore. A signal cannon boomed among the shaded trees, and war drums sounded on both sides. From the left charged a company in red armor, led by Qin Ming, the “Thunderbolt.” From the right charged a company in black armor, led by Huyan Zhuo, the “Double Clubs.” Each commanded five hundred mounted troops, and together they cut the invaders off at the water’s edge. By the time Liu Menglong hastily called for more soldiers to leave the ships, more than half his officers and men had already fallen. Hearing the battle cries from the vanguard, Niu Bangxi ordered the rear vessels to withdraw for the moment. Then a rapid series of cannon blasts sounded from the mountaintop, and a rushing noise arose among the reeds. It was Gongsun Sheng, hair unbound and sword in hand, pacing the Dipper’s pattern and performing rites on the summit to summon the wind. At first it pierced woods and trees; then stones rolled and sand flew. In moments white waves towered to the sky, black clouds covered the earth, the red sun lost its light, and a furious gale arose. When Liu Menglong hurriedly ordered the ships turned about, small craft emerged from the reed beds, the depths of the lotus flowers, and every narrow creek and inlet, rowing straight into the formation of great warships. At the sound of the drums, all the men lit their torches. In an instant a great fire sprang up, its fierce flames soaring to heaven. The small boats scattered in every direction and darted among the larger vessels, setting all the government ships, fore and aft, ablaze. How terrible was that rising fire? Behold:

p.src: Black smoke shrouded the green waters; red flames rose from the clear waves. The raging wind swept lotus leaves flying across the sky; the advancing fire scorched the reed beds and snapped their stalks. Gods howled and ghosts wailed; in the murk, the sun gave no light. Peaks shook and mountains crumbled; the vast roar of the waves seemed filled with wrath. Warships and boats all capsized; rudders and oars alike were useless. At the sterns, banners could no longer be distinguished in their mingled colors; upon the towers, swords and halberds could no longer be arrayed like crossing frost and snow. Corpses floated beside fish and turtles; hot blood boiled together with the waves. A thousand tongues of flame rose to meet the sky; ten thousand trails of smoke skimmed over the water.

p.src: When Liu Menglong saw flames flying throughout the harbor and all the warships ablaze, he had no choice but to cast off his helmet and armor and leap into the water. Not daring to approach the shore, he chose a place where the channel was deep and broad and swam away for his life. From within the reeds, a lone man came straight toward him, handling a small boat by himself. Liu Menglong dived beneath the surface, only to be seized around the waist by another man and hauled aboard the boat. The boatman was Tong Wei, the “Cave-Leaving Dragon,” and the man who seized him around the waist was Li Jun, the “River-Muddling Dragon.” Meanwhile, seeing fire break out on every side among the government ships, Niu Bangxi also threw off his military garb and armor and was about to enter the water. Just then a man rose from the stern, caught him squarely on the head with a boat hook, and dragged him backward into the water. That man was Zhang Heng, the “Boatman.” Across Liangshan Marsh, corpses covered the water and blood spattered the waves; those scorched and burned beyond recognition were too numerous to count. Dang Shiying alone escaped in a small boat, but as he rowed away, crossbow bolts and arrows flew together from both sides of the reed beds and shot him dead in the water. Of the many soldiers, those who could swim escaped with their lives, while all who could not were drowned. Those taken alive were all bound and sent to the main stronghold. Li Jun had captured Liu Menglong, and Zhang Heng had captured Niu Bangxi. They meant to escort the pair up to the stronghold, but feared that Song Jiang would release them again. The two heroes conferred and killed both captives there by the roadside. They cut off their heads and sent them up the mountain.

p.src: Meanwhile, Grand Marshal Gao was leading his troops in support along the water’s edge. Hearing a rapid series of cannon blasts and an unbroken roll of drums, he guessed that battle had begun on the lake. Spurring his horse, he rode forward to a place beside the mountain overlooking the water. He saw soldiers in droves fleeing through the water and scrambling ashore. Gao Qiu recognized them as his own men and asked what had happened. They told him that fire had destroyed all the ships and that no one knew where the others were. At this, Grand Marshal Gao grew still more alarmed. Seeing black smoke fill the sky and hearing battle cries without cease, he hurriedly led his army back along the old road. But when drums sounded before the mountain, a troop of cavalry charged out to bar his way. At their head was Suo Chao, the “Impatient Vanguard,” who swung his great mountain-cleaving ax and galloped straight toward him. Wang Huan, a military governor at Grand Marshal Gao’s side, leveled his spear and rode out to engage Suo Chao. Before they had exchanged five bouts, Suo Chao wheeled his horse and fled. Grand Marshal Gao led his troops in pursuit, but after they rounded a spur of the mountain, Suo Chao had already vanished. As they continued onward, Lin Chong, the “Panther Head,” led troops up from behind and attacked them in another fierce clash. They had gone no more than six or seven li when Yang Zhi, the “Blue-Faced Beast,” led another force after them and attacked once more. Before they had fled another eight or nine li, Zhu Tong, the “Lord of the Beautiful Beard,” overtook them from behind and attacked yet again. This was Wu Yong’s strategy of pursuit: rather than block the enemy from the front, he attacked only from behind. The defeated troops had no heart to fight; intent only on fleeing, they could give no aid to their rearguard. Thus Grand Marshal Gao was driven on in panic and fled at full speed to Jizhou. By the time he entered the city, it was already the third watch of the night. Then he heard that fires had broken out in the camp outside the city, where battle cries continued without end. It turned out that Shi Xiu and Yang Xiong had placed five hundred infantrymen in ambush. They set three or five fires and slipped secretly away. Grand Marshal Gao was so terrified that his soul nearly left his body. He repeatedly sent men to investigate, and only when they returned to report that the raiders had gone did he feel relieved. When the troops were mustered and counted, more than half had been lost.

p.src: While Gao Qiu was still perplexed, a scout came from afar to report, “The imperial envoy has arrived.” Gao Qiu led his troops and the military commissioners out of the city to welcome him, and on meeting the envoy learned of the edict offering amnesty and submission. They were all introduced to Staff Adviser Wen Huanzhang, then entered the city together to deliberate at headquarters. Grand Marshal Gao first obtained a copy of the edict and examined it. If he refused the amnesty, he had already lost two battles in succession, while all the boats he had commandeered had been burned to ashes; yet if he accepted it, he was ashamed to return to the capital. He wavered at heart and could reach no decision for several days. Now in Jizhou there was an old clerk named Wang Jin. So vicious was he by nature that everyone called him “Heart-Gouging Wang”; he was a clerk assigned by the Jizhou prefecture to serve at headquarters. Having seen the copy of the edict and learned that Grand Marshal Gao remained undecided, he went to headquarters to propose a useful stratagem. “Your Excellency need not hesitate,” he reported. “This humble clerk sees that the edict itself offers a way out. The Hanlin drafter who composed it must be well disposed toward Your Excellency, for he has already left you a back door.” Gao Qiu was astonished and immediately asked, “How can you tell that he left a back door?” Wang Jin replied, “The most crucial part of the edict is a line in its middle. It says: ‘Excepting Song Jiang, Lu Junyi, and all the others, great and small, their crimes and misdeeds shall alike be pardoned.’ As written, this is an ambiguous sentence. But when it is read aloud, divide it into two sentences. Read ‘Except Song Jiang’ as one sentence, and ‘Lu Junyi and all the others, great and small, shall alike be pardoned for their crimes and misdeeds’ as another. Lure them unsuspectingly into the city, seize Song Jiang, their chief, and kill him. Then break up all his followers and transfer them separately to different places. As the old saying goes, ‘A snake cannot move without its head, nor a bird fly without its wings.’ Once Song Jiang is gone, what use can the rest be? What does Your Excellency think of this proposal?” Gao Qiu was delighted. He at once promoted Wang Jin to chief secretary of headquarters, then summoned Adviser Wen and told him of the plan. Wen Huanzhang remonstrated, “An august imperial envoy must deal with men according to upright principles; deceit must not be practiced upon them. If some resourceful person among Song Jiang’s company sees through the trick and they turn against us, the consequences will be most unfavorable.” Grand Marshal Gao said, “You are wrong! From ancient times the military texts have said, ‘Warfare follows the way of deception.’ How could one conduct it with open rectitude?” Adviser Wen replied, “Though warfare indeed follows the way of deception, this concerns an imperial edict, by which the Son of Heaven wins the trust of all under Heaven. Since ancient times a sovereign’s words have been as binding as the silken cord; hence they are called the Jade Voice and may not be altered. If we act in this fashion now, once it becomes known, no one will ever again regard an edict as trustworthy.” Grand Marshal Gao said, “We shall deal with the present need first and worry about the rest afterward.” Thus he refused to heed Wen Huanzhang’s counsel. He first sent a man to Liangshan Marsh to notify Song Jiang and his entire band to come before Jizhou city, hear the Son of Heaven’s edict, and receive pardon for their crimes.

p.src: Now Song Jiang had once again defeated Grand Marshal Gao in battle. He ordered the lesser officers to haul away the burned boats for firewood, while the unburned vessels were seized and taken into the naval stockade. All officers and soldiers captured alive were released one after another and sent back to Jizhou. That day, while Song Jiang was deliberating with all the chiefs in the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness, a lesser officer reported, “A messenger from the Jizhou prefecture has come up the mountain with news: ‘The court has specially dispatched an imperial envoy bearing an edict to pardon your crimes and accept your submission, granting you offices and noble ranks. I have come expressly to bring these glad tidings.’” On hearing this, Song Jiang felt as though joy had fallen from Heaven, and his face lit up with smiles. He ordered the messenger brought into the hall and questioned him. The man said, “The court has issued an edict expressly offering you amnesty and submission. Grand Marshal Gao sent this humble man to report and request that every chief, high and low, come before Jizhou city, perform the prescribed rites, and hear the edict proclaimed. There is no hidden difficulty; please harbor no doubts.” Song Jiang summoned the military strategist and settled the matter with him. He then brought out silver and bolts of silk to reward the messenger and sent him back ahead to Jizhou. Song Jiang issued orders that every chief, high and low, prepare to go and hear the edict proclaimed. Lu Junyi said, “Brother, do not act hastily. I fear this is some scheme of Grand Marshal Gao’s; you should not go at once.” Song Jiang replied, “If all of you remain so suspicious, how can we ever return to the right path? Whatever comes of it, we must make the journey.” Wu Yong laughed. “That scoundrel Gao Qiu has been so thoroughly beaten by us that his courage is shattered. Even if he has ten perfect schemes, he cannot put one of them into effect. With this whole company of heroic brothers at hand, harbor no doubts; simply follow our elder brother Song Gongming down the mountain. I shall first send ‘Black Whirlwind’ Li Kui with Fan Rui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun, leading one thousand infantrymen, to lie in ambush on the eastern road from Jizhou. Then I shall send ‘Ten Feet of Steel’ Hu Sanniang. She will lead Gu Dasao, Sun Erniang, Wang Ying the Short Tiger, Sun Xin, and Zhang Qing, with one thousand infantrymen, to lie in ambush on the western road from Jizhou. If they hear a rapid volley of cannon fire, they are to charge toward the north gate and join forces with us.” Once Wu Yong had completed these deployments, all the chiefs descended the mountain, leaving only the naval leaders to guard the stronghold. Grand Marshal Gao sought to use deceit to lure this band of heroes down from the mountain and ignored Adviser Wen’s remonstrance; but who could have imagined that the ground below Jizhou city would instead become another battlefield before Mount Jiuli? Indeed: A single edict from the sovereign stirred the hearts of the whole band of heroes. How the heroes ultimately raised havoc in Jizhou will be revealed in the next chapter.
